rewrites.25937730: Recovery logic assumed capacity waiting to be refilled. Arrivals fell to 80,400 in FY20/21. The task was to refill idle seats, rooms and routes. That slack is gone. rewrites.25503CD6: Cape Town did more than refill its seats. It added 17 mainline international routes between 2015 and 2025, more than any of eight peer airports. The Aviation Market Assessment now asks what comes next. The rebound that a recovery plan is built to capture has already happened.[^20]
rewrites.689B9970: Interest in the destination is large and the share that becomes a visit is small. A survey of 34 outbound markets counts 97 million high-value travellers interested in South Africa, of whom 1.4 million arrive [[QUERY Q11: 1.4 million arrivals where, and in which year?]]. The Market Assessment concludes that the challenge is converting interest into visits, not generating demand.[^22]
rewrites.4C9AE1B3: **Long-haul distance and cost.** Every large overseas market is a long-haul flight away. Most visitors must connect to reach the province. The four hub routes through Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa and Istanbul carried 53% of arrivals on the ten largest routes. No non-stop service links Cape Town to India or China. A direct Indian route is unlikely before 2030. The Aviation Market Assessment expects carriers to raise fares on full routes before they add seats. In SA Tourism's 2020 brand tracker for the USA, 30% to 50% of respondents at each stage said the country was too expensive to reach and 27% to 47% said it took too long. This report holds no fare or trip-cost series by market.[^24]
rewrites.23B0BFA4: **Safety perceptions.** Safety is the barrier travellers name first. The barrier research (2024) ranks crime and personal safety first and visa and entry requirements second. The evidence ranks the perception but does not measure its effect on bookings.[^25]
rewrites.2C0B5BC5: **No reason to travel now.** The destination is desired but deferred. In the US tracker 70% of respondents were aware of South Africa and 7% were considering a trip in the short term. Among the small group that had sought information but planned no trip soon, 37% said another destination appealed more. No source measures deferral directly or when interested travellers mean to book. Dates do move decisions: Chinese outbound bookings peak around the main holiday periods. Dated events, seasonal moments and limited offers give a traveller a reason to book this year (section 3.1).[^26]
rewrites.313FA9B1: **Reluctance to self-drive.** Beyond the Metro and the Garden Route the province is effectively car-only, so a visitor who will not drive sees little of it. Accessibility falls from 4.7 out of 5 in the Cape Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo. Even the Garden Route has no shuttle between its towns. Chinese travellers favour structured itineraries that keep logistics simple. No source measures how many long-haul visitors decline to drive or why.[^27]
rewrites.6FA03B97: **Difficulty finding information.** A traveller who decides to come still has to assemble the trip. Itineraries, transfers, what is open, what is safe and how to buy it are hard to find on the platforms each market uses. Chinese, Indian and Gulf travellers plan and book on their own platforms. Gulf travellers find no Arabic-language booking or local-currency pricing. Bookability is one part of this barrier. A desk test found regional rooms listed online, while named attractions outside the core had no standalone online ticket.[^29]
rewrites.03F5AF42: Seats pace growth at the summer peak, not across the year. International routes ran 76.0% full on average in the year to November 2025. rewrites.5D57A47B: Outside the peak there is room and traffic there has grown faster. Comparing 2024 with 2015, monthly international passengers rose by an average of 88% in the airlines' summer season of April to October and 73% in their winter season of November to March. Growth in the quieter months does not wait for runway relief.[^34]
rewrites.61849C4E: Global tourism grows 3% to 5% a year under stable conditions, the band the benchmarking work calls organic growth. In 2024 the world grew 11% as recovery ran on. Only Chile at 40.4% and Singapore at 21% grew far faster. The longer record is the better test (section 2.2). Santiago's airport grew from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019, at least 5.5% a year.[^36]
rewrites.376D3A39: The Western Cape's two cases straddle the band. The base case implies 3.8% a year from 2025 to 2035 and the accelerated case 5.3%. The accelerated case reverts to base unless routes are confirmed. The benchmarking work counts growth as structural only above that band and only when deliberate changes to demand drivers, access or product drive it, not cyclical recovery or short-term promotion.[^37]
rewrites.60AEEFDA: The action plan aims at 2.5 million international arrivals by 2035, 5.3% a year on the accelerated case and just above the world's norm (sections 1.1 and 2.1). Growth above trend is rare across whole regions; where it happens, it is specific to a destination. Benchmarking asks which deliberate choices let comparable destinations outgrow the world and which of them the Western Cape can adapt. It looks for how each destination removed what bound its growth, not for isolated good practice.[^39]
rewrites.3234746F: The yardstick is the world's own growth. Growth of 3% to 5% a year is the norm under stable conditions; above 5% marks structural acceleration and 10% or more a structural shift. UN Tourism puts global growth at 11% in 2024 (while recovery was still running) and about 4% in 2025. Growth counts as structural only when deliberate changes to demand drivers, access conditions or product systems drive it, not cyclical recovery or short-term promotion. Each case was read for its demand profile, two proven growth levers and how far they transfer to the Western Cape.[^40]
rewrites.135FB8A1: Each destination received one average score across the twelve criteria and the 30 were ranked on it. Chile, Melbourne and Victoria, Valencia and Singapore came from the top of that ranking. Partial likeness ruled out others in the upper half. Namibia lacks city, wine and cultural depth. Reykjavik and Iceland sell one nature product with extreme seasonality. The Eastern Cape and Garden Route have no long-haul hub or global brand role. The screen chose on likeness to the Western Cape, not on growth, so a comparator can teach stability as well as speed.[^42]
rewrites.16FB1EE1: The six cover the constraints the province faces. Chile and New Zealand show how a gateway wins long-haul seats and fills them; Singapore shows how hub traffic becomes visits and Kenya how a gateway carries visitors beyond its best-known product. rewrites.2625A6C8: Only Chile and Singapore grew far faster than the world in 2024: Chile by 40.4% and Singapore by 21%, against the world's 11%. Neither rate proves structural growth. Melbourne's 4.3% is an Australia-wide forecast rather than an actual. The lessons that follow come from what the leaders built over a decade, not from one year's rate.[^44]
rewrites.6B0EFB4D: Against global growth of 11% in 2024, only Chile and Singapore grew far faster and three of the six were still below 2019.
rewrites.20123FA6: The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors. The province has its own precedent above the 5% mark. International two-way passengers at Cape Town International rose from 1.71 million in 2015 to 3.1 million in 2024, about 6.8% a year. Most of the rise came before COVID-19: traffic grew about 11% a year from 2015 to 2019 and about 3.5% a year from 2019 to 2024, inside the norm. The faster years followed the forming of the Cape Town Air Access partnership in 2015. It counts 33 route launches since; 16 more destinations were served in 2025 than in 2015, close to the 17 mainline routes in the peer comparison above. Outside a recovery, 2015 to 2019 is the province's own case of growth above the norm.[^45]
rewrites.27F5F738: Chile was chosen as a long-haul city gateway to coast, wine and wilderness, with Mediterranean seasons like the Western Cape's. South America supplies 55% to 60% of its arrivals. Yet long-haul access was its binding constraint and Chile treated it as infrastructure. A private concession won in 2015 funded about US$900 million of expansion, under one of the world's most liberal aviation systems built on open-skies agreements. Direct routes now link Santiago with Europe and Australia. A domestic network carries visitors on to Patagonia and the wine valleys. Santiago's airport traffic rose from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019. The lesson is blunt: tourism demand follows air access.[^46]
rewrites.3C9FBE45: Kenya is the African case, chosen for its long-haul reliance, regional dispersal and community-based tourism. African markets supply 41% of its arrivals, while long-haul visitors spend more per head. Kenya made conservation part of its national economic infrastructure, joining wildlife protection, tourism and community participation in one governed system. It positioned Nairobi as East Africa's aviation, diplomatic and business hub. Its main airport now carries 68% of arrivals. Despite meaningful reforms, fragmented investment and regulatory hurdles remain ongoing challenges. Kenya earned about US$1,460 per international arrival in 2024, against about US$890 for the Western Cape.[^49]
rewrites.57E54962: Events do the same work across the calendar. The Western Cape has the green-season gap they address (section 2.3). rewrites.7E5B535F: The benchmarking work reduces that system to three components. Each comparator builds its own around a different anchor (Figure 2.4).
rewrites.4096DE6F: Five community cases ask what keeps tourism income in townships and rural settlements. Each matches one of four types among the province's 107 long-listed communities. The types turn on two facts: whether a community lies within 45 minutes of a tourism node and whether it holds an attraction. Vilakazi Street in Soweto and Santa Marta in Rio de Janeiro speak to communities near a node whose assets are underused. Kliptown speaks to communities near a node with no attraction of their own. Comuna 13 in Medellín, remote by access rather than distance, speaks to remote communities with assets. Costa Rica's rural network speaks to remote communities without them.[^60]
rewrites.76E01559: Cape Town's route record was set against eight peer airports: Calgary, Christchurch, Edinburgh, Keflavik, Larnaca, Marrakech, Santiago and Valencia. Santiago targets tripling its passenger volumes in twenty years.[^61]
rewrites.4B55A69F: Between 2015 and 2025 Cape Town added 17 mainline international services, more than any of the eight peer airports. Santiago added 14 services, Valencia 12 and Calgary 8. At Cape Town, the Aviation Market Assessment sees low-cost entry as a longer-term opportunity. The Western Cape does not need to learn how to win mainline routes. rewrites.08476B20: The cases show what worked elsewhere; they cannot prove it will work here. Singapore's tourism board answers to one ministry, in a system strongly directed by the state yet closely tied to the private sector. The Western Cape works across three tiers. rewrites.36E56C6A: The evidence also has gaps. No score by criterion is reported. Among the six only New Zealand (3.67) and Kenya (3.50) have a reported score. Its Tourism Development Framework reports uneven past progress and links it to restructuring, thin resources, little support from other departments and weak monitoring. That is a plan, not a destination, so the gap remains. Several comparator charts are unlabelled, so only reported figures are quoted here. Valencia's figures name no primary source. The route-support recommendation drawn from Chile carries no amount. None of the cases holds Western Cape data, so the province's side of each comparison comes from sections 2.3 to 2.5. rewrites.578A38D6: **Objective 4, Convert India and China hub traffic; objective 6, Build a regional foundation (Africa).** Singapore's joint strategy with its airport and airline; Kenya's hub strategy and African base.
rewrites.34C71635: **Objective 7, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes; objective 15, Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies.** Chile's airport concession and air access fund; New Zealand's route-tied marketing. rewrites.5A7FCFB9: **Objective 11, Align visitor experience in-destination; objective 3, Make the whole province findable and bookable.** Valencia's governed quality and certification visible on booking platforms.
rewrites.7450C00D: **Objective 13, Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion.** Resident sellers outlasted the programmes that launched them. Capital built before an operator, as in Kliptown, earned no operating income.
rewrites.4DDB063F: Interest in the Western Cape is broad and converting it into visits is the first task. The demand that does arrive is concentrated in a few mature markets and the peak season. rewrites.2F644A12: The fall and the climb were both steep. Arrivals dropped to 80,400 in FY20/21 and 378,500 in FY21/22, then returned to 1.07 million in FY22/23. rewrites.18029C07: No other province shown earns spend ahead of its arrivals. Across the same quarters Gauteng took 41% to 44% of arrivals and 39% to 48% of spend. rewrites.6E17B197: Kenya earns the most per arrival of the destinations compared and the Western Cape ranks third (Figure 2.5).
rewrites.78A7D7F2: Length of stay is a growth lever in its own right and its measures disagree. SA Tourism's departure survey puts the average international tourist's stay in the Western Cape at 12.5 nights in 2025, against 14.8 nationally and 13.0 in the province in 2023. Mobile-location data puts international tourists at 2.9 days in Cape Town in 2025 and 3.0 in 2023, when 31.5% stayed one day. The survey bands in the Demand-Side Analysis show 5% staying 1 to 2 days, 12% staying 3 to 4 and 14% staying 7 to 10, on bands that sum to 48%.[^77]
rewrites.63098CD8: The three measures count different things and this report does not choose between them. The departure survey divides bed nights by tourists and covers every purpose of visit across the province, long family stays included. The mobile data follows a sample of devices in the city alone and counts day visits. The survey bands describe about half their sample, since 52.33% of respondents gave no length of stay. No source gives nights in the province by market, apart from single readings of 10.9 nights for Chinese tourists and 9.4 for Indian tourists in 2024.[^78]
rewrites.783707AE: Many long-haul visitors divide a South African trip between provinces. On the 2025 departure survey 9% of international travellers visited more than one province, but about a third of North American, German and French visitors did. Multi-province travellers averaged 20 days against 14 and spent about three times as much; 59% of them took part in wildlife experiences. One large tour operator suggests a minimum of three nights in Cape Town and three on safari. For these visitors Cape Town is one leg of the trip. The question is how many nights the city and the regions win.[^79]
rewrites.697C8C2E: Section 2.1 sets out the gap between interest and visits and the six barriers behind it. The market shares show how wide that gap is in each core market. rewrites.1F26F5A1: The province takes under 0.3% of air outbound trips in every core market and fewer than three in ten Indian or Chinese visitors to South Africa reach it.
rewrites.1B0BAFF7: Four values-based segments make up the interested travellers counted in section 2.1. Each has priority markets: Curious Explorers in the UK and the USA and Creative Connectors in India. Discerning Connoisseurs are paired with China and the UAE and Reflective Adventurers with Germany.[^82]
rewrites.4C1214E4: Each segment is most concentrated in a named set of markets and Discerning Connoisseurs spend most on a long-haul trip.
rewrites.5790559C: Curious Explorers and Discerning Connoisseurs align best with the Western Cape's offering. The segments also matter for spread, not only for volume. Curious Explorers offer the strongest opportunity to spread visitors beyond Cape Town. Reflective Adventurers can ease seasonality through year-round outdoor and wellness travel. These two are the segments to target for the regions and the green season.[^83]
rewrites.2F6097D7: Stakeholders describe the same travellers from the product side. SATVITO sees an opening with cultural travellers if the province packages its cultures, township and village experiences included. CapeNature finds its international appeal concentrated in eco-adventure niches such as hiking and bouldering. The Overberg District reports rising demand for remote experiences. Both fit the two segments named for the regions and the green season.[^84]
rewrites.31EC9E7A: Five markets supply 63% of overseas arrivals: the UK, Germany, the USA, the Netherlands and France. The three largest alone held 52% in 2025 and no market outside the five reached 3% (Table 2.6).[^85]
rewrites.3DDCF3F5: Source: 2024: Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25 and p32 (Wesgro Visitor Tracking Survey 2024; shares sum to 100%). 2025: Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12 (Stats SA and SA Tourism 2025; the printed shares sum to 104.9% and the October to March share is computed with the 2025 shares normalised to 100%).
rewrites.06C42315: Supply follows the same curve. June carries 6.4% of 2025 international seat capacity into Cape Town. Airlines cut seats across the green season. Growth depends on converting more interest into visits from April to September, not on pushing more demand into the peak months. Filling those months needs seats as well as conversion (section 2.4).[^93]
rewrites.76A78ADB: Green-season traffic has doubled since 2015 and its share of the year rose to 41.6% in 2023 before easing.
rewrites.7485ACD0: Rooms tell a more cautious story than the terminal. Cape Town Tourism's hotel sample averaged 61.7% occupancy in 2025 and reached 81.5% in February. More room stock, shorter stays or residents travelling out could each explain the gap. An analyst estimate points the same way for the regions. May to September room-night demand grew 22% in the Cape Winelands and 31% on the Garden Route from 2015 to 2025, against 17% for the year in each. Its panel is not published.[^94]
rewrites.245341DD: The green season is also not one season. May to August is the core winter. April and September are shoulders with different products and buyers [[QUERY Q16: which months?]]. Google reports that search data can show when potential travellers research destinations, which would give seasonal campaigns an evidence base.[^95]
rewrites.7169DE6E: There is material to build on. The City's This Is Cape Town campaign runs in 55 cities on six continents. Wesgro's April 2026 memorandum with Emirates names growth markets but sets no targets for regional nights. Recognition beyond Cape Town (and nights there) is the missing link between demand and dispersal.
rewrites.1278311E: Only the accelerated case assumes direct routes to India and China and it alone clears 5% growth a year.
rewrites.6EF871F7: Only the accelerated case clears the norm. From the 2025 base of 1,498,829 arrivals, the base case's rate sits within the 3% to 5% norm and the accelerated case alone passes the 5% mark of structural acceleration (Table 2.9; section 2.2).[^99]
rewrites.3253219B: The six mature markets grow at 2% to 4% a year. The USA adds more arrivals than the UK from a smaller base. The UK grows with outbound travel on strong direct access. Germany's slower growth reflects a weaker economic outlook. The USA runs above its long-term outbound trend on recent demand and a favourable exchange rate. The Netherlands is a loyal repeat market and France has room to gain share from low penetration, while Switzerland rests on a seasonal direct service.[^102]
rewrites.6111A1FF: The acceleration markets grow fastest from the lowest base. India and China with Hong Kong each more than double. The Middle East and Brazil grow by more than half. Japan and South Korea are modelled separately as strategic markets: small today, high in spend and dependent on future routes and awareness.[^103]
rewrites.612A4897: Recent arrivals run the other way. Stats SA counted 75,541 Indian and 41,651 Chinese tourists to South Africa in 2024, then 69,680 and 37,902 in 2025. Industry views attribute the fall to air access, price and trade confidence as well as entry rules. The model's 8% a year stands as the base case and the decline is carried as context and risk. The 2027 starting point has not been retested against the decline.
rewrites.4FABAF3E: Regional markets give the model its steadiest growth. Namibia and Zimbabwe stay the core and add the most arrivals, while Kenya grows fastest on East African connections and rising outbound demand. rewrites.1D99FA7C: India adds the most arrivals of any market and the USA the most among mature markets.
rewrites.139FCF41: The growth markets are already in the air, on other carriers. rewrites.59B924F7: Chinese travellers discover destinations on short video and decide inside booking platforms. rewrites.14C99F43: India is among Cape Town's largest unserved air markets. Addis Ababa and Dubai carry 81% of Indian travellers and half of them start in Mumbai. rewrites.74DEABA7: The Middle East is both a source market and the province's main gateway. Dubai is the largest route into Cape Town and Doha the third largest. rewrites.2ECBEC67: Each market meets a readiness gap once it looks closer: little Mandarin service, few visible vegetarian options or Indian-language guides and no Arabic-language booking or local-currency pricing. rewrites.6038E8A2: The province's own channels also lag. rewrites.24A76576: Closer to home, Africa already supplies a large and steady base. rewrites.1016161E: Spend ranks the markets differently. African visitors spent R4.2 billion in the province in 2025. Zimbabwe and Namibia supplied R1.94 billion of it. rewrites.7069F482: Business travel has recovered worldwide and is still growing. rewrites.2BA972CA: Business events lift spend and can be scheduled. International business-event delegates to South Africa spend R6,400 a day on average. rewrites.3B1BAE55: Cape Town leads Africa in the one segment that is measured. It ranked 35th in the 2024 ICCA ranking. rewrites.4A5AF6E4: Regional spread does not need the main event to move. rewrites.3348C3A5: Public money for events is small and tied to other purposes. DEDAT's R7 million Tourism Growth Fund for 2026/27 supports attraction and business development, not event hosting. rewrites.46721EC3: Stakeholders raised demand less often than supply or capability and rated it lower. rewrites.61B9EDA8: Three messages run through the summary statements. Growth should go to under-visited regions and the green season, not to flagship sites under pressure, yet activation is too weak to smooth demand. Marketing and digital capability lag international practice. Destinations do not package proximity and itineraries before travellers book flights. The mature markets remain the base but have had too little international marketing, while activation in India, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific is too thin to turn early interest into visits.[^128]
rewrites.5686F0B0: Individual organisations sharpen these points. CapeNature takes about 70% of reservations through its call centre, because its product is too complex to book unaided. SATVITO finds the offer perceived as concentrated on icons such as the wine route and Table Mountain. Robben Island Museum finds China and Japan absent from its top source markets. On the USA two organisations are more cautious than the model: the CTICC reports softer North American association demand after US funding freezes and the Cableway sees a recovery with limited momentum.[^129]
rewrites.54E74AB6: The demand evidence points to three tasks and conversion comes first. Each growth market discovers, weighs and books travel differently, so broad destination marketing alone will not turn interest into visits. The work is to put the province inside each market's own platforms and trade, with itineraries, languages and payments to match.[^130]
rewrites.14010C09: The third task is access and it paces the peak, not the year. The growth markets stay underconnected and the hub carriers remain the working gateways. More frequency from Emirates, Qatar Airways and Ethiopian comes first, with long-term route cases for India and China behind it. Conversion work and seat retention can start now; route cases follow as runway capacity arrives (section 2.4).[^132]
rewrites.56A71751: **Objective 4, Convert India and China hub traffic.** About 101,000 hub journeys a year reach Cape Town. A direct Indian route is unlikely before 2030. The model has both markets more than doubling by 2035, yet national arrivals from both fell in the first nine months of 2026. On SA Tourism's count, fewer than three in ten Indian or Chinese visitors to South Africa reach the province.
rewrites.633661B4: **Objective 5, Increase yield in mature markets.** Five markets supply 63% of overseas arrivals and the highest spend per visitor. The model grows them at 2% to 4% a year. The province takes under 0.3% of their air trips. The USA gains share while the UK, Germany and France lose it.
rewrites.384F2A15: **Objective 6, Build a regional foundation (Africa).** Zimbabwe and Namibia supply 62% of 323,971 African tourist arrivals. Nigeria and Kenya hold the largest modelled pools. Nigerians and Ghanaians spend as much per visit as mature-market visitors.
